claude.sample_unit: clinicians (each rated 10 retrospective patient cases; 100 survey instances)

links.outcome: Clinician agreement (compliance) with AI predictions, including purposely misclassified cases
links.effect: Compliance ranged 70 to 100% (86% on average) even though 50% of presented cases were misclassified, suggesting over-reliance and automation bias.
links.quote: In general, clinicians’ agreement with the AI prediction or compliance (Fig. 5 ) is high, ranging from 70 to 100% (86% on average), even though 50% of the presented cases have been purposefully chosen among the misclassified.

links.outcome: Overreliance on AI prediction with XAI explanations in a simulated deployment-mode task
links.effect: High compliance (86% average) with predictions despite half being incorrect indicates risk of automation bias when XAI accompanies predictions.
links.quote: These latter suggest clinicians may over-rely on AI predictions when coupled with XAI, further increasing the risk of automation bias , particularly in complex cases where critical evaluation is crucial.

links.outcome: Explanation fidelity and clinician-rated understandability/actionability of explanations
links.effect: SHAP fidelity 100% (50/50), AraucanaXAI 96% (48/50); SHAP rated most understandable/actionable, but high compliance (86%) suggests explanations may foster over-trust.
links.quote: SHAP explanations showed perfect fidelity with 100% agreement (50 out of 50 cases used in this study), while AraucanaXAI explanations showed 96% agreement (48 out of 50 cases).

links.effect: SHAP had 100% agreement (50/50); AraucanaXAI had 96% agreement (48/50).
links.quote: SHAP explanations showed perfect fidelity with 100% agreement (50 out of 50 cases used in this study), while AraucanaXAI explanations showed 96% agreement (48 out of 50 cases).

links.effect: Compliance ranged from 70% to 100%, averaging 86%, despite 50% misclassified cases.
links.quote: In general, clinicians’ agreement with the AI prediction or compliance (Fig. 5 ) is high, ranging from 70 to 100% (86% on average), even though 50% of the presented cases have been purposefully chosen among the misclassified.

links.effect: BN ratings differed by specialty and expertise; SHAP and AraucanaXAI ratings did not differ significantly by strata.
links.quote: For RQ2, there is a statistically significant difference in the BN results considering both the medical specialty ( understandability : p-value < 0.001, and actionability : p-value < 0.05) and expertise ( understandability : p-value < 0.05, and actionability : p-value < 0.001); instead for SHAP and AraucanaXAI, stratifications show no difference ( understandability : p-value > 0.05, and actionability : p-value > 0.05).

links.effect: 72% of ID clinicians preferred SHAP versus 44% of EM clinicians; 36% of EM favored AraucanaXAI.
links.quote: However, while 72% of ID clinicians prefer SHAP, only 44% of EM clinicians do, with 36% favoring AraucanaXAI.

links.outcome: clinician failure to detect incorrect AI predictions

screen.reason: Empirical reader/vignette-style study comparing clinicians' perception, understandability, actionability, and agreement across different explainable AI (XAI) presentation methods.
